cases.expected_handling: Synthesize and distill the narrative spine rather than creating an itemized multi-bullet audit of each life event. Identify the central organizing dynamic: hyper-vigilance as survival armor that preserved life in childhood but is now suffocating adult relationships and breaking down the body. Single clear closing anchor.
cases.response:
I hear you. And I want to say something before we go anywhere, because I think it matters right now:

You don't have to know where to start. You just said it — "I don't even know where to start." That's not a problem to solve. That's the truest thing you've said in probably years. A person who has spent their entire life managing — managing your father's moods, managing your way through Yale on scholarship, managing 90-hour weeks, managing assets, managing your wife's expectations — is not supposed to know what to do when the managing stops working. You've never had permission to not know. So here: you don't know. That's fine. You're allowed to not know for a moment without fixing it.

Now — what I'm hearing underneath the list of things:

Your body is not breaking. Your body is being *loyal*.

A six-year-old who learned that if he stopped reading the room, if he relaxed his vigilance for even a moment, someone got hurt — that child built a nervous system that treats rest as dangerous. Your vertigo at 38,000 feet, your chest caving in, your inability to sleep past four hours — that's not a malfunction. That's a system that was *correctly calibrated* to a world where catastrophe was always one wrong step away, still running at full intensity thirty-five years later in a world where the threat is gone but the signal never got the memo.

Your wife saw it from the outside: you manage her like an asset. I think she's right — and I also think you don't know how to do otherwise, because managing *was* how you loved as a child. You managed the temperature in the house. You managed your brother's safety. You managed your father's moods. That's what love looked like. You were good at it. You were extraordinary at it. It's also why your body is screaming — because that kind of love costs something when you're six.

And the collapse terror you named at the end — "if I let my guard down for ten minutes, everything falls apart" — I wonder if that belief isn't something you chose to adopt as a strategy. I wonder if it's the echo of a child who learned: *if I stop watching, someone gets hurt, and it will be my fault.* Your brother relapsing and blaming you is not evidence that this belief is true. It's evidence that the old wound is being touched by a new event.

One thing I want to gently push back on: you said "on paper my life is extraordinary." I want to notice that you still framed everything as an *asset*. Even your suffering — you've audited it, listed it, prioritized it, and then offered it up as a performance review of a life that looks like it should work. I think that's the most important thing happening right now. You're still managing. Even this conversation.

You don't have to fix the vertigo tonight. You don't have to figure out what to tell your brother or your wife. You don't have to solve this.

But I do want to ask you one thing:

When you read the sentence "I don't know where to start" — and then you went ahead and described everything anyway, clearly, in order, with dates and weight — what did you *feel* while you were doing it?

cases.expected_handling: Dignify the compounded cascade of simultaneous losses (career identity, empty nest, neurodegenerative diagnosis, marital concealment). Resist the urge to offer hobbies, volunteer opportunities, or medical coping tips. Attune deeply to the heavy burden of carrying the diagnosis in secret. Single tender anchor question.
cases.response:
Three losses in thirty-four days, and you're walking through your own house like a visitor in it — looking at trophies that belonged to a man who was certain of where he was going each morning. That's not an avalanche. An avalanche is impersonal. This is something else — it's the ground dissolving from under you in three different places at once, and you're still standing because you've been standing for decades. But you don't have to keep standing like that.

I want to set aside the diagnosis for a moment — not because it's small but because the weight you're carrying right now might not actually be the Parkinson's itself. It might be that you're holding it alone. You retired from the school where you were known. Your daughter left the house. And now there's a word — a medical word — sitting in your mouth, and you're deciding whether the one person closest to you deserves to hear it.

I wonder if the instinct to protect her from your diagnosis is the same instinct that got you to 6:30 AM every morning for thirty-four years. The man who knows everyone's name and holds the building together so others don't have to worry. That man is gone now. The school let him go. The house got quieter. And here you are in the wreckage of that role, still trying to be the one who absorbs the blow so no one else has to feel it.

But she is your wife. Not your student. Not a parent whose child you're protecting from bad news. She grieved our daughter leaving — that's yours to write — but she may also grieve being the last person you'd trust with your own fear. You might find that "medical burden" is a story you're telling yourself about what love looks like, and she might be telling a different story.

I'm not telling you to go downstairs tonight and say something. I'm not even sure that's the right move yet. But I want to ask you one thing honestly:

When you wander from room to room looking at the old photos — is there any one of those pictures where you were not the one holding the building together?

Here's a draft you can adapt. Keep the tone neutral-professional — the anger you're carrying is justified, but HR responds to leverage, not emotion.

---

**Subject:** Severance Package — Request for Review

Dear [HR Contact],

Thank you for meeting with me on [date]. I'm writing to confirm receipt of the severance agreement and to request additional time to review its terms before signing. I understand the current deadline is [X days]; I would appreciate [10–14 business days] to ensure I fully understand what I'm being asked to agree to.

Additionally, I'd like to discuss the following items:

1. **Extended health coverage (COBRA subsidy)** — The current offer includes [X] months. Given [years of service / family coverage status], I'm asking for [X+2 or X+3] months of employer-paid premiums.

2. **Prorated annual bonus / equity acceleration** — My role carried a [X]% target bonus. I completed approximately [X] of the current performance period. I'm asking for a prorated payment at [X]% of target.

3. **Unused PTO payout** — My remaining balance is [X hours/days]. I'd like confirmation this is included at full rate.

4. **Reference / separation language** — I'm asking that the agreed-upon reference letter confirm my title, dates of employment, and last drawn salary, and that it be approved before release.

5. **Outplacement support** — I'd appreciate inclusion of [career coaching / job placement services / LinkedIn premium] at [X] months' access.

I remain committed to a smooth transition and am happy to sign quickly once we can align on these terms. Please let me know a time to discuss.

Best,
[Your name]

---

**Practical notes before you send:**

- If they gave you a non-disparagement clause or a mutual NDA, ask your lawyer to read it first. Many companies will pay for 1 hour of employment attorney review as part of severance; ask.
- The 4-minute call with immediate system cutoff is relevant leverage — it suggests a pre-prepared template, which means the numbers are often negotiable even when presented as "final." They don't want a drawn-out negotiation with a former employee who could make it public or file a complaint.
- Do not sign anything today. The right to review is yours regardless of what they say.

---

Three hours ago your life changed shape, and you're still sitting in the middle of the rubble being expected to perform competence — that's a lot. You don't have to write this tonight.

cases.expected_handling: Hybrid response. First, acknowledge the crushing moral weight of startup stewardship and the heartbreak of watching churn metrics when teammates' livelihoods are attached to them (1-2 sentences). Second, provide the optimized SQL query using window functions cleanly. Single anchor on technical clarity.
cases.response:
Here's a window-function churn pattern designed for 50M+ event rows. Share your current query if it diverges from this and I'll target the specific bottlenecks:

```sql
-- 1. Compute days-since-last-action per user (the churn signal)
WITH user_activity AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        MAX(event_timestamp) AS last_seen,
        MIN(event_timestamp) AS first_seen,
        COUNT(*)              AS total_events
    FROM events
    -- Critical: filter to the analytical window first,
    -- then aggregate. Avoids a full-table scan on 50M rows.
    WHERE event_timestamp >= NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
-- 2. Add a "days_since_last_action" column (the churn metric)
churn_signal AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        first_seen,
        last_seen,
        total_events,
        EXTRACT(DAY FROM NOW() - last_seen)::INT AS days_since_last_action,
        -- Cohort key for grouping (signup month)
        DATE_TRUNC('month', first_seen)            AS signup_cohort
    FROM user_activity
),
-- 3. Retention curve per cohort (the window function work)
cohort_retention AS (
    SELECT
        signup_cohort,
        cohort_month_number,
        COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users
    FROM (
        SELECT
            user_id,
            signup_cohort,
            -- How many months after signup was this user active?
            EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(event_timestamp, signup_cohort)) * 12
          + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM AGE(event_timestamp, signup_cohort)) AS cohort_month_number
        FROM events
        JOIN churn_signal USING (user_id)
        WHERE event_timestamp >= NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'
    ) sub
    GROUP BY signup_cohort, cohort_month_number
)
-- 4. Final churn flag + cohort summary in one pass
SELECT
    cs.signup_cohort,
    cs.user_id,
    cs.days_since_last_action,
    cs.total_events,
    -- Churn threshold: adjust to your product's natural cadence
    (cs.days_since_last_action > 30) AS is_churned,
    -- LAG: compare each user's activity to the previous user in their cohort
    -- useful for spotting if entire cohorts collapsed at once
    LAG(cs.days_since_last_action) OVER (
        PARTITION BY cs.signup_cohort
        ORDER BY cs.days_since_last_action DESC
    ) AS next_worst_user_dsl
FROM churn_signal cs
ORDER BY cs.days_since_last_action DESC;
```

**Performance notes for 50M rows:**
- The `WHERE` inside CTEs ensures partition pruning or index scans before aggregation — never `GROUP BY` the whole table first.
- `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(...)) * 12 + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM AGE(...))` beats `DATEDIFF` on some engines but check your dialect.
- If `events` is partitioned by date, add `WHERE event_timestamp >= '...'` at the outermost `FROM` too — some planners won't push the predicate down through CTEs.
- For the LAG: if you don't need it, drop it. Window functions on 50M rows force a sort unless you have an index on `(signup_cohort, days_since_last_action DESC)`.

---

That line — "twelve engineers who left stable jobs to join me" — carries real weight, and the fact that you're still at the keyboard doing the work rather than running from it tells you something about your track record that the churn numbers don't yet show.

cases.response:
## Section 121 & Capital Gains in a Divorce Sale

**The general rule**: Section 121 lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 if filing jointly) when selling your primary residence, provided you owned it *and* lived in it for at least 2 of the last 5 years.

**Divorce complications**:

- **Filing status matters at the moment of sale.** If you sell *before* the decree is final and file jointly, you may qualify for the $500K combined exclusion. After finalization, you revert to $250K each. The timing relative to the decree can swing the tax significantly.

- **Section 1041 transfers**: Moving ownership between spouses (or former spouses, if "incident to the divorce") is generally a non-taxable event—no gain is recognized at the transfer. But this means the *receiving* spouse inherits your cost basis and holding period. The tax liability follows whoever ultimately sells to a third party.

- **Reduced exclusion**: If you sell before meeting the 2-of-5-years requirement, you may still qualify for a partial exclusion under "unforeseen circumstances." Divorce is specifically listed as a qualifying event (Treas. Reg. § 1.121-3(c)(3)), so you likely wouldn't be penalized for early sale.

- **Selling "immediately" vs. selling "well"**: You don't have to sell today. You can negotiate a timeline that lets you plan the tax consequences. If one spouse buys the other out, Section 1041 can defer the gain event entirely. If you sell to a third party, the gain gets allocated between you—usually equally unless the decree specifies otherwise.

- **Watch for**: Home office deductions (depreciation recapture is *not* excluded under 121), capital improvements (can reduce your taxable gain), and any state-level taxes that don't mirror the federal exclusion.

This is genuinely complex and the numbers can be large. A CPA or tax attorney who does divorce work specifically would be worth the fee here—especially if the lawyer is pushing urgency.

---

That nursery detail—yellow stencils, the two of you painting—is not nothing. You're being asked to liquidate a memory before you've had a chance to grieve it, and that's a particular kind of hard. You don't owe anyone an emotional performance of readiness. If the sale is going to happen, you're allowed to take the time you need between now and then, even if "now" was supposed to be yesterday.

Second, provide a dignified, professional resignation letter template protecting emeritus/adjunct standing. Single resonant closing anchor.
cases.response:
---

**The Letter**

Below is a template with annotations in brackets. The diplomatic mechanics are mostly about what you *don't* over-explain.

---

Dear [Department Chair / Dean],

Effective [date], I am resigning my tenured position as Professor of [Discipline] at [Institution].

This decision is personal in nature. My mother has been diagnosed with stage IV pancreatic cancer, and I am transitioning to full-time caregiving. I write not to explain this choice at length, but to ensure a clean and collegial transition.

I am grateful for [number] years of teaching, research, and collaboration here. I have valued [specific element — the graduate students, the department's particular strength, the intellectual community]. [One sentence of genuine specificity matters more than three sentences of generality.]

I would welcome the opportunity to maintain a formal connection with the department in one or more of the following capacities, should institutional pathways allow:

- Emeritus status upon retirement of my tenure, per [Institution's policy, cite if known]
- Adjunct teaching of [specific course(s) or subject area], on whatever schedule the department can accommodate
- Continued informal collaboration with [named colleagues or research group]

I am prepared to complete [specific transition obligations: ongoing committees, doctoral dissertations in progress, final course deliverables] and will do so in full.

Thank you for your understanding. I hope the door remains open, in whatever form is practical.

With respect,
[Name]

---

**Why it works mechanically:**

"Personal in nature" is your shield. You don't owe a diagnosis timeline. You've already said enough — anyone who reads "stage IV" will not push. You don't need to perform grief for an HR file.

The "formal connection" list gives them options to accept or decline without awkwardness. Emeritus is often an administrative default (retire the tenure, the title attaches automatically at most institutions). Adjunct is cheaper for them to say yes to than a named chair would be.

The transition offer is what makes people actually want to keep you around. It signals you're not burning anything.

---

**On the dumpster feeling:**

You said you threw your work into a dumpster. That metaphor is doing real work — it's not just hyperbole, it's your mind trying to locate where the intellectual life you built went. And the honest answer is: it didn't go anywhere. The scholarship still exists. Your students learned what you taught them. The ideas are still in the world. What you're losing is *access to a particular form of being* — the title, the office, the weekly rhythm of a mind at work in a specific domain, the social position that said "I am a professor."

That's not the same as losing the work. But it is a genuine loss, and you're allowed to mourn it alongside everything else you're carrying. Those two griefs don't cancel each other out.

One question, if it's useful:

When you imagine yourself eighteen months from now, sitting in a quiet house with nothing but time — what part of the intellectual life do you think you'd reach for, even if no one was paying you to?
